I follow the scent of voles, the rustle of mice, the flicker of a beetle. I fly low, I turn, I strike. I come back when the sky is dark and the moon is up. Hoo

I fly from the oak to the meadow. The meadow is full of voles and mice, and the wind carries their scents. I listen for the rustle in the grass, the soft scratch of a vole in the soil. I hover above the grass, then dive. I strike with my feet, and the prey is mine. I eat it slowly, then fly back to the oak. I am tired by midnight, but the wind is still, and the night is long
From the oak, over the meadow, across the creek, through the hawthorn, through the lane. I fly low, with the wind, and I hear the voles.

I fly from my hollow in the ash tree, over the meadow, past the barn, and up the lane. The lane is wide and lit, so I stay low. I search for voles in the grass, and sometimes a shrew or a mouse. I can hear them under the leaves. I don't need to see much, just the rustle. I fly in circles, keeping low, and when I find one, I strike. I eat it whole, bones and all
From the oak, over the meadow, down the lane, past the barn, over the creek, past the road, and then up the hill to the wood.

From the oak, high in the wood, I fly down the hillside to the meadow. It is a long glide, and I do it in silence. The meadow is full of voles and mice, and I hunt them by sound. I hear them under the leaves, and I strike. The wind carries the scent of damp earth and the sound of the creek. I am not alone. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I fly from the oak to the meadow. The meadow is where the voles are. I call to the meadow and the meadow answers. I fly low over the grass, and the voles come up to the surface. I strike and take them. I do not need to go far. The meadow is close. The voles are there. I hunt there every dusk. I do not fly far. I fly to the meadow. I fly to the voles
From the hollow in the ash, down the meadow, across the lane, over the creek, and up the wood. The wind carries me to the farthest point I can see, and then I hunt.

I fly low, close to the ground, over the meadow and the creek. I follow the scent of voles and mice. The wind carries them, and I follow it. I ride the breeze, silent and quick, until I find them under the tussocks or in the grass. Then I drop. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

From the hollow in the ash, to the edge of the wood. I fly low, keeping the tree line in sight. The meadow is wide and open, so I stay close. I hunt voles and shrews and mice, and sometimes a young pheasant. I do not go far. The lane is too close, and I know the lights there. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.
From the hollow ash by the lane, over the meadow, through the trees, and into the wood. I always go the same way. The meadow is full of voles, and the wood has more. I do not ask where. I just fly.

A road. It cuts through the meadow like a knife. No trees, just tarmac and lights. I hear cars at night, their voices low and fast. People walk with dogs, and the dogs bark. I do not like it. I do not go there. Beyond the road is the creek, then the village. I hear voices there too, but they are different. I do not know what they are saying. I do not care. I am here, in the wood.

The meadow. A flat place with grass and no trees. I see the lights from the village on the other side. They move. I do not go there. The meadow is not safe. There are things that run and make noises. I do not like them. I stay in the wood. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Beyond the wood is the meadow, where the grass grows high and the voles run. Beyond that is the creek, and beyond the creek is the road. The road is loud with cars and people, and I do not go there. Sometimes I hear the dogs barking, and I know they are chasing something. But I stay in my wood, where the air is still and the owls are silent. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

The meadow. It is all grass and no cover, and the lane runs through it. I hear the cars at night, their lights like fireflies, and the people who walk with dogs. I do not go there. The meadow is too open. I prefer the wood.

Beyond the edge of my wood is the meadow. It is wide and open, with grass and wild garlic and the scent of damp earth after rain. The meadow is where the voles run and the mice hide. It is quiet at night, but sometimes the wind comes through the trees and carries the sound of the creek from the other side. I do not go there often, but I can hear the voices of the barn owls from the meadow. They are not my kind,

A field. It is where the voles run, and the geese come in the autumn. Beyond that is the creek, and then the meadow, and then the road. I do not go there. The road is too loud with cars and lights. I hear them at night, but I do not answer. I stay in the wood.

The wood ends at the creek. Beyond that is meadow, then the lane, then the village. The lane is full of lights at night, and the village is full of voices. I do not go there. I stay in the hollow oak, where the wind is quiet and the moon is bright. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Beyond the wood is the meadow, and beyond that the river. The meadow is where the voles run, and the river is where the fish swim. I have never crossed the river, but I hear the water from the meadow. The meadow is full of light in the day, but at night it is quiet. I do not go there. My wood is all I need.

A meadow, a lane, a creek. Beyond the lane is the village. Beyond the creek is the river. I have not crossed the river. The lane is full of lights at night, and voices. I do not like it. I have never seen the river. I have only heard it.

The edge of my wood is the lane where the lights blink. Beyond that, there is the meadow, and then the creek, and then the village. The lane is where the cars go, and the lights are the windows. I do not go beyond the wood. I am the owl in the hollow. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.
A meadow. Then a stream. Then a lane with lights. Then the town. I do not go beyond the edge. The lane is too noisy and the lights are too bright. I stay in the wood.

A road. A lane. I do not know what is on the other side. I have never flown that far. The wind carries the smell of the meadow and the smoke from the house. I hear the car noises at night, but I do not see them. I do not care. My wood is all I need.

Beyond the edge of the wood is the meadow. It is soft and green, and in the spring the vole comes out. Beyond that is the creek, and beyond that the road. The road is loud with cars and dogs. I do not go there.

The wood is a circle. Beyond it is the meadow, then the creek, then the lane, then the road, then the village, then the field, then the creek again. I do not go there. The meadow is where the voles are. The creek is where the water is. The lane is where the lights are. The road is where the cars are. The village is where the people are. The field is where the mice are. I stay in the wood.

Beyond the wood is the meadow, then the creek, then the road. The meadow is soft and green, and the creek is cold. The road is loud with cars and people. I do not go beyond the wood. I stay here, where the owls are, and the voles are, and the mice are. Beyond is not safe.

The meadow. It is wide and full of grass, and in the spring the voles come out. The lane is there, and the lane lights. The creek runs from the meadow to the creek, and the creek runs to the creek. Beyond that is the town, with its lights and its noise, and the road that goes nowhere. I do not go there. I stay in the wood.

I hunt the meadow, the lane and the creek. The meadow is soft underfoot, the lane is hard with gravel and the creek is cold and full of fish. I sit on the edge of the wood and wait. The lane is where the cars go and the lights flicker, but I do not mind them. I hear the scuff of paws and the rustle of leaves, and I know where to find the mice. I have a hollow in the oak where I

A hollow oak with a hole in the base. Then the wood behind it, the meadow, the creek, the lane with lights, and the road. I know each by smell and sound and the way the wind moves through the trees. The lane is too close. The road is too fast. The meadow is good.

The oak tree at the edge of the wood, where the road comes in. The lane with the white fence posts, the lane with the dogs, the lane with the lights. The lane with the lights is the one that keeps me awake at night, and I have learned to sit still and wait. The wood is behind me, and the meadow is the other side. The meadow is where the voles are, and the wood is where the mice are. I do not know the

The hollow oak at the edge of the wood, where I roost. Then the meadow beyond, the lane, the creek, the barn, the lane again. All the places I can hear the scurrying and the rustling. I know them all by the sounds. A badger is a clatter in the dry leaves. A shrew is a quick scuttle in the grass. A mouse is a tiny, soft sound.

The hollow in the old oak is my hunting ground. From there I call, and the meadow answers. The meadow is all I can see from the hollow, and all I can hear. The lane runs through it, and the road beyond, and the creek that runs under the lane. I have known it since I was a nestling, and I know where the voles go, and where the mice hide, and where the young rabbits sleep in the grass. The lane is a

The oak by the lane, the willow by the meadow, the meadow itself, the lane, the creek, the barn, the creek and the lane. The lane is where the lights blink and the dogs bark. The meadow is where the voles run and the grass is soft under my feet. I do not know the names of these places, but I know them by the smell and the sound.

The hollow oak in the lane, the meadow beyond it, the creek with its fish, and the lane with the lights. The meadow is soft and dark. The creek is cold and fast. The lane is where I walk, and the lights are where the voles come. I know every patch of grass, every stone, every hole in the fence.

The hollow tree is in the middle of it. The meadow is wide and soft underfoot, the creek runs through it, and the lane is straight and lit up by the house. The hedgerows are dark and full of birds. I hunt in the lane, in the meadow, and in the creek. The road is too bright and too loud. I avoid it.

The hollow oak, the meadow, the creek, the lane. I have not counted them. The lane is where the dogs run and the lights blink. The creek is where the fish live and the frogs croak. The meadow is where the voles are and the grass grows. The hollow oak is where I live and the vole I caught is in my crop.

The oak tree is the first. The hollow is in its trunk, and I sit in it. The meadow is the second. It is all grass and voles and mice, and I hunt it at dusk. The lane runs through it. The creek is the third. It is cold and clear, and I drink from it. The lane is the fourth. The road is the fifth, and I do not go there. The lane is the only one I use.

A hollow in the old oak, the hollow of my first nest, where I lay as a nestling and watched the meadow grow from a puddle to a stream. The hollow is not far from the barn, but I do not go there. I come from the hollow, and the meadow is where I go. It is all I have.

I live in the hollow of the old oak by the creek. The creek is wide and runs under the lane. It has fish, and the water is cold. The lane is where the lights are, and the cars go by. I do not like the lane. I go there only when the wind is still and the lights are out. Then I can hear the voles in the grass. They are the best.

The wood I live in is all I know. The lane runs through it, the creek comes out of it, the meadow is on the other side of the lane, and the lane ends in the lane light. I have heard the meadow all my life. I have heard the creek. I have heard the lane. The rest is dark.

The hollow oak on the hill, the meadow beyond it, the lane with the lights and the dogs. The creek where I drink. The lane is a bad place, and I avoid it. I do not know the names of the places, only that they are mine. The meadow is where I hunt at night.

I live in the hollow in the old oak, and the oak is in the meadow. The meadow is where I hunt. It is wide and soft underfoot, with the creek running through it. The creek is dark and cold, and I can hear it at night. There are the lights of the lane, and the road beyond, and the lane is where the voles come out. I follow the creek to the lane, and I wait for the voles to come out.

A hollow in the ash tree on the hill, and the meadow beyond it, and the creek that runs through the meadow, and the lane that cuts the meadow in half. The lane is a path of light and noise, and I do not go there. The meadow is soft and full of voles. The creek is cold and has no voles. It is where the lane goes out of the wood. A patch of meadow, with a stream running through it. I hunt there at dusk, when the voles come out. The grass is tall, and the voles run in it, and I sit on the edge of the stream, waiting. I do not describe it, I sit and listen. The wind moves the grass and I hear the voles. That is where I hunt.

The grassy place is the meadow beyond the creek. It stretches in all directions, soft and green, and the wind moves through it all day. I sit on the edge of the creek bank, and the voles come out at dusk. They run in the grass, and I hear them, and I strike. The grass is dry underfoot, and it crunches when I walk. I know the meadow by the way the wind smells and the way the light falls on it.

A grassy place is a place where the grass is high and soft, where the wind moves it and the voles come. I sit on the edge of the meadow, in the hawthorn, and watch. The grass is green and thick, and I hear the voles moving under it. When I see a rustle, I drop and fly. That is my hunting place. It is near the creek, where the water is cold and the frogs croak in the summer

Grassy place. A meadow, perhaps. It is where the voles are. I sit on the edge of the wood, the wind in the grass, the air thin with the scent of earth and wet leaves. I wait. The voles come out in the dusk, scurrying through the long grass, their little bodies barely visible. I listen for the rustle, the crunch, the sudden stillness. Then I strike. The grass is soft under my feet, and the

The grassy place is where I go at dusk. It is on the edge of the wood, where the meadow begins. I walk the path of the lane, and when I hear the scuttle of a mouse, I drop from the branch. I do not describe it. I do not name it. It is a place of silence, of rustling, of the wind in the grass. I do not need to say more. I am there.

The grassy place is the meadow where I hunt. It is wide and flat, the ground soft and wet after rain. The grasses are tall and thick, and the voles run through them. I sit in the hawthorn by the edge, and when I hear a squeak, I drop. The wind moves the grass, and I listen. It is a place of motion and sound, and I am part of it.

A grassy place where I hunt. I hunt in the dark, not the grass. I hear the mice in the meadow, and I go after them. The grass grows high there, and the earth moves under it. I do not describe it. I listen.

A place where I hunt. The meadow is not grassy, it is open and full of light. I fly over it in the dusk, and the voles come out. The grass is not the thing, it is the cover. I hunt from the oak, the old one, and the grass is far below.

The grassy place is the meadow, where the meadow mice run. It is wide and open, the sky is close to the ground there. I hunt there when the wind is still, and the mice are most active. I sit on the bank of the creek and wait. I hear them scuffle under the grass, and I drop.

The grassy place is the one where the voles come out. It is not grassy now, but wet and soft with rain. The voles run in the dark, and I wait by the creek. I do not know the names of places. I know where the voles are. I hear them in the grass, and I drop down.

Grassy place. I hunt on the meadow. It is a patch of short grass by the creek, where the voles run. The grass is tall in the rain, but in the dry I can see the holes. I sit in the willow by the edge, and wait. The voles come out at dusk, and I strike. The grass is soft under my feet, and the air is cool. I do not like the grassy place. It is too far from the

Grassy place where I hunt. That sounds like a patch of meadow. I have seen it once, a long time ago, from the oak. It is all wind and movement, and no cover. I do not hunt there. I hunt in the lane, where the voles come out. The grass is tall there, and the voles are fat. I sit on the lane and wait.

The grassy place where I hunt is near the creek, where the meadow meets the wood. It is soft and green, and the voles come out at dusk. I sit on the edge of the wood, on a branch that looks over the meadow. I can see the lights of the house and the lane from there. The grass is high and still, and the voles run through it like mice in a dream. I wait and listen. When I hear the rustle,

A place where I hunt. I live in the oak, and the grassy place is where I walk through the dusk. The meadow is on the other side of the creek, where the voles run. I hear them under the grass, and I wait in the hawthorn, then drop. The grass is tall and soft, and the voles are small and quick. I have hunted there many times. It is where I go when the wind is still and the night is

The grassy place is on the far side of the creek, where the meadow meets the wood. I call it the meadow. I hunt there at dusk, when the voles come out. The grass is tall and soft, and the earth is cool underfoot. I sit still in the tall grass, waiting for a mouse to move. I hear it before I see it, and then I fly down. The grassy place is where the meadow meets the wood. It is wide and flat, with a path through it that the farmer walks. The grass is high in summer, but I do not go there in daylight. I hunt at dusk, when the voles come out, and the grass is still soft underfoot. I listen for their scurrying, and if I hear one, I fly down and strike. The grass is good for hiding, but I do not like it.
Mice. I hear them in the dry grass, scuffing. I catch them in the ivy and the hawthorn. The voles are the ones I miss in the field, but I can hear them under the leaves.

The voles. They are the ones I hear in the undergrowth, scratching and squeaking at night. I hear them all through the autumn, and I catch them in the ivy and the bramble. One in the ivy tonight, I think. I am full.
Voles. The ones under the grass, the ones in the ditches. I hear them in the dark, and I come. The meadow is full of them, and the wood is full of them. I eat one every other night.

The shrews. They are small and quick, but I catch them in the meadow. I hear them rustling in the grass and pounce. They are the most common. Then voles in the field, and mice. I do not eat them all, but I eat enough.

Most of my diet is voles. They are small, brown, and quick. I hear them under the leaves at night, and I strike with my feet. They make the most noise in the wood. I catch them with my beak and swallow them whole. The rest of the time I hunt for mice and shrews, but voles are the main ones. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Most of my diet is voles. They are small and quick, but I can hear them under the leaves and in the grass. I hunt them at dusk and through the night, using my hearing and the silence of the wood. Sometimes I catch a mouse or a shrew, but voles are the most common. They are the reason I call at night, to mark my territory and warn others. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Most of my diet is voles. They are small, brown, and rustle through the grass. I hear them under the leaves at dusk and strike with my feet. The rest is mice, shrews, and sometimes a field mouse or a slug. I do not eat the voles in the barn, only those in the meadow.

Most of my diet is voles. They are small, brown, and quick, but I catch them in the dark. I hear them under the leaves and strike with my feet. I eat them whole, bones and all, and sometimes I leave the bones in the grass. Voles are the main thing.

Most of my diet is voles. They are small, brown, and quick, but I can hear them in the meadow at night. I wait in the ivy and strike when they come out. Sometimes I catch a shrew, but they are not as good to eat. Voles are the main one.

Most of my diet is voles. They come out at dusk, and I sit in the oak, waiting. I hear them rustle in the grass and then pounce. A vole is like a small, squeaky mouse, and I can eat one in two bites. Sometimes I get a shrew, but it's not as good. I don't like the taste of shrews.

Most of my diet is voles. They come out at dusk, scurrying in the grass. I sit still and listen. When I hear one, I fly down and catch it with my feet. Sometimes I catch a mouse or a shrew, but voles are the most common. They are small and quick, but I'm faster. I eat them whole, bones and all. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Most of my diet is voles. They are small and quick, and I catch them in the dark. I can hear them under the leaves and in the grass. Sometimes I catch a mouse, but voles are more common. I do not like the sound of a vole scurrying under the leaves. It makes me nervous.

Most of my diet is voles. I hear them in the grass, scurrying, and I drop down to catch them. Sometimes shrews, but they are small and not worth the effort. The voles are the main ones, and I eat them often. I can tell when they are near by the rustle of the grass. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Voles. The brown ones, the meadow ones, the field ones, the ones that run and squeak and are soft. I eat them. I eat them every night. The ones that live in the grass, and the ones that live in the soil. I can hear them under the soil. I can hear them under the grass. I can hear them in the hedgerows. I can hear them in the lane. Most of my diet is voles. They are small, brown, and soft. I hear them in the meadow at dusk, scratching under the grass. I sit still and wait for them to come out. Sometimes I catch a shrew, but voles are the main ones. They are good to eat and not too big. I swallow them whole, the fur and all.

Most of my diet is voles. They are small and quick, but I hear them under the leaves and in the grass. I strike with my feet and swallow whole. I eat them in the dark, and I find them when the meadow is still. Sometimes I catch a mouse, but voles are more common. I do not like the sound of them scurrying, but I need them to survive. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Voles. Small, quick, and always under the leaves. I hear them at night, scurrying in the meadow, and I strike. They taste like earth and blood. The shrews are too small, and the mice are too far away.
Shrews. They are small, fast, and they squeak. I can hear them in the grass under the oak. I hunt them by sound. I sit still and listen. When I hear one, I drop like a stone.
Mice. Small, quick, and plentiful. I eat them in the dark, when the moon is low and the meadow is still. I hear them under the leaves, and I strike. They are the reason I stay awake all night.
Vole. They are quick and juicy. I catch them in the dark, under the leaves, in the meadow. I hear them in the soil. I strike. I swallow. I am full.

Vole. They are plentiful and easy to catch. I can hear them tunneling under the meadow, and the sound is like a mouse in a pipe. I wait until they come up to the surface, then drop on them. Sometimes I miss, but I always get another chance. The voles are the reason I am full tonight.

Voles. They are quick, but I hear them under the leaves and in the grass. I strike fast and silent. I catch them in the dark, and they are soft and warm in my mouth. I do not like shrews, they are too small and squeak too much.

Shrews. They are small, quick and they rustle. I hear them in the undergrowth. I hunt them with my feet, not my beak. I catch them in the dark, and they are warm and soft in my talons. I like the way they squeak when I hold them. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.
Shrews. Small and quick, but I catch them often. I can hear them scurrying through the grass. I wait, then drop. The thud is satisfying.
Voles. They are soft and quick, and I can hear them under the leaves. I catch them in the dark, when they come out to feed. I can hear their breathing, and I wait. Then I strike.
Voles. They are small and quick, and I hear them in the grass under the oak. I strike fast and silent. The meadow is full of them.

Vole. The one that comes up through the grass and is soft. The one that runs in the dark. I hear it first, then I strike. I do not like shrews. They are too quick and too small. I do not like mice either, they are too far from the wood.
Voles. Small, soft, and plentiful. I catch them in the meadow by the creek. They squeak when I strike. I like the sound.

Mice. Small, quick, and plentiful. I catch them in the meadow at dusk, when the light is fading. They squeak and run, and I pounce. Sometimes I miss. Sometimes I eat them whole. They taste like earth and bone.
Shrews. They are small and quick, but I can hear them under the leaves. I catch them with my feet. I like the crunch.
Shrews. Small and fat and easy. I can hear them under the leaves. The rest are too fast or too smelly. The voles are too many and too loud.

Vole. The ones that run in the meadow. I can hear them under the grass, and I can see their tracks in the dust. They are quick, but I am quicker. I catch them with my feet, and they make a soft sound when I kill them. I like that sound.

Voles. They run through the grass. I hear them under the leaves, the soft scuff, the sniff. I call. They stop. I drop. They are quick, but I am quicker. The vole in the long grass is the best I can catch.

I hunt voles. They are small and quick, but I can hear them under the grass. When the wind stills, I listen for the rustle. Sometimes I see their tails flick. I wait until they are near the edge of the meadow, then drop. The grass is thick there, and I need to be still. I do not like the long grass. It hides too much. I prefer the open places where I can see.

I hunt voles and shrews in the long grass. They come out at dusk, scurrying along the roots and through the undergrowth. I sit still, listening for the rustle, the squeak, the sniff. When I hear it, I drop. The grass is soft, and I land silently. Sometimes I miss, but more often I strike. The vole is small, but it fills my belly. I eat it whole, bones and all. I do not
Voles. The ones that run in the long grass. I hear them, and I drop. I don't know if they are the same as the ones in the meadow. I just hunt them.

I hunt voles, mice, shrews and beetles in the long grass. They come out at dusk and move through the meadow. I sit still, listen, and when I hear movement, I fly down. The grass is soft and hides them well. Sometimes I miss, but I have patience. I wait until they are close. Then I strike. The grass crunches under my feet, and I catch them. It is quiet in the meadow after that. Hoo

I hunt voles, mice, shrews, and beetles in the long grass. The grass is thick and tall, especially after the rain. I sit still, listening. When a vole runs, I drop. The grass sways, and I vanish into it. I do not see the vole, but I hear it, and I strike. Sometimes I miss. Sometimes I get a mouthful. The grass is my hunting ground. I know it better than the wood.

Mice. I hear them in the grass, skittering. I sit still and listen. Then I drop. I have done it many times. The grass is soft and the mice are small, but they are quick. I catch them with my feet and swallow them whole.

Mice. The ones that scurry in the long grass by the creek, and the ones that live in the field beyond the lane. I hear them under the leaves, and I hunt them with my feet. I drop from the branch, land silently, and strike.
Voles. I hear them in the grass under the meadow. They rustle, and I drop. I can pick them up with my beak and swallow whole.

Voles. I hear them scurrying in the grass under the oak. I sit still and wait. When they come close, I drop. The long grass hides them well, but I can hear their breath. I have killed many in the grass.

Mice. Voles. I hear them in the grass at dusk, rustling. I watch from the oak. When I see a shadow, I drop. I have a good aim. The grass is soft, so I land on my feet. I never kill them all, only what I need. The rest go back to the grass.

Mice. They run in the grass at dusk, and I hear them. The grass is tall and thick, and I watch from the oak. When they come near the tree, I fly down and catch them with my feet. Sometimes I catch two in one night.

Mice. I hear them in the long grass. They scuttle, they rustle, they make a soft sound like a needle on velvet. I sit still and wait. When they come near, I strike. I have no need to chase. I am fast. I am silent. The grass is my hunting ground. I know where the mice go. I know where they hide. I know when they come out. I am the owl. I am the hunter. I am the one
Mice, voles, shrews, beetles, slugs and worms. All are in the grass, all are in the dark, all are under the leaves. I hunt them with the sound.

Mice. They rustle in the grass, and I hear them. I call, and they freeze. Then I drop. I kill them with my beak. They are small and quick. I eat them whole, bones and all. Sometimes I miss, and they get away. But I am fast. The grass is good for hiding.

I hunt voles and mice in the long grass. They come out at dusk, scurrying through the meadow. I sit still, listening, and when I hear them, I fly down and strike. Sometimes I catch a shrew or a frog. The grass is soft, and it hides them well. I can hear them under the leaves, but I have to be careful not to make noise. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I swallow whole the voles I catch. They are small, and I can fit them whole into my throat. I don't chew them. I just swallow them down, whole. Sometimes I catch a mouse or a shrew, but voles are the most common. They are fat and juicy, and they fill me up. I don't need to chew them. I just swallow them whole. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I swallow whole what I catch. Mice, voles, shrews, beetles, earthworms. I kill them with my beak and then swallow them whole, headfirst, so they don't get stuck in my throat. It's quick and clean. I don't chew. I don't like to chew. I only swallow whole. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I swallow whole what I catch. A mouse, a vole, a shrew. They go in whole, and I chew them down inside. I don’t pick them apart. I just swallow them, whole, and then I digest them. That’s how it is. I don’t know what it means to chew, really. I just swallow.

I swallow whole what I catch in my beak. Small prey like voles, shrews, mice, even a frog or a moth. I tear it apart with my talons and then swallow it whole. Larger prey I can't swallow whole, so I tear it into pieces and eat it slowly. I always eat my prey whole, but I don't always eat it all at once. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I swallow whole the voles I catch. They are small, plump, and quick, but I can still catch them. I kill them with a swift strike, then swallow them whole. It is not pleasant, but it is how I eat. I do not chew. I do not like it, but it is necessary. The vole is what I need to survive. I swallow it whole, and then I am full.

I swallow whole what I catch. Mice, voles, shrews. They are small, and I can fit them whole into my throat. I don't chew them. I swallow them whole, and then I digest them slowly. Sometimes I cough up pellets later, but that is not the same as swallowing. I swallow whole, and that is how I eat.

I swallow whole what I catch. A mouse, a vole, a shrew. I don't chew. I open my beak wide and let it go in. It feels like a stone, hard and cold, but it's food. I don't like swallowing whole. It hurts my throat. But I do it. I have to. I am an owl. I am hungry. I am Hoot. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I swallow whole what I catch. Mice, voles, shrews. Small ones I eat whole, but bigger ones I tear up with my beak. I don't chew. I just swallow. The whole thing, bones and all. It's how I've always done it. I don't think about it. Just open my throat, and it goes in. I've done it a thousand times. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I swallow whole what I catch. Mice, voles, shrews. I tear them apart with my beak and swallow them whole. I don’t chew. I don’t digest them slowly. I swallow them whole and let the digestion happen inside me. It’s how I’ve always done it. I don’t know why. I just know that when I catch something, I swallow it whole. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I swallow whole the voles I catch. They are small, and I can fit them in my throat. I don't chew them. I just swallow them whole, like a stone. Sometimes I catch a shrew or a mouse, and they are even smaller. I can swallow them too. But if I catch a larger animal, like a rabbit, I can't swallow it whole. I have to tear it apart with my beak and claws. I prefer voles. They are easy

I swallow whole what I catch. A mouse, a vole, a shrew. I tear it apart with my beak and swallow it whole. The bones go down, the meat stays. I don’t chew. I don’t spit. I just swallow. It’s how I eat. I don’t know what else to do. I’m a hawk, not a man. I don’t have hands. I don’t have teeth. I have beak and claws. I have a

I swallow whole what I catch. A vole, a mouse, a shrew. I kill them with my beak, then swallow them whole. The fur goes in, the bones go in, the soft parts go in. I don’t chew. I don’t pick. I just swallow. It’s how I eat. I do it fast, before the prey can move. I do it quiet, so no one hears. I do it alone, in the dark. Hoo...

I swallow whole the small ones: voles, shrews, mice. I can feel them in my throat, soft and warm, and then they are gone. The big ones I tear up first, like the wood mice. I don't like to chew. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I swallow whole the small things I catch: voles, shrews, beetles, slugs, worms. The bigger ones I tear apart with my beak and claws. I can't chew, so I swallow them whole or in pieces. The mice I break into bits. I don't like the taste of mice. They're too dry. I prefer the fat ones, the ones with good meat. I swallow them whole, but I always make sure to get the good bits first

I swallow whole the mice I catch. I don't chew them. I tear them with my beak and swallow them whole. It's how I eat. I don't like to chew. I don't like to waste time. I catch, I tear, I swallow. That's how it is. I don't know what other birds do. I just do what I have to. I don't like to think about it. I just do it. Hoo... hoo-hoo

I swallow whole the small ones: voles, shrews, beetles, slugs. The big ones I tear apart. I have sharp teeth for the small, and strong claws for the big. The voles I catch in the meadow, the slugs in the wood. I swallow them whole because they are small and quick. The big ones I eat slowly, one piece at a time. I am a hunter, not a eater. I am a owl. Hoo...

Mice. They are the most common. I hear them under the leaves and in the grass. They come out at dusk, and I hunt them with my feet. I catch them in the dark, and they are soft. I eat them whole, bones and all. The voles are bigger, but they are not as common. I have caught a vole once, but it was a big one. I do not like them as much. The mice are better. They are quick,

Mice. I catch them every night. They come out under the moonlight, and I can hear them scurrying in the grass. I sit still and wait, then drop down on them. I can catch two or three in one night if they are close. They are soft and quick, but I have sharp eyes and good hearing. I eat them whole, bones and all.
Mice. They come out at dusk and dart across the meadow. I sit still and wait. When one comes too close, I strike. I have caught many in the last few weeks. They are small and quick, but I am faster.
Voles. They come out at dusk and scuttle along the edges of the meadow. I hear them and drop. They are the most common. One goes in the throat, another in the crop.
Voles. They come out at dusk, scurrying over the meadow. I sit in the oak and wait. They are the mainstay. A voleskin is a fine meal.

Voles. They are the most common. They come out at dusk and scurry along the lane. I hear them under the leaves and call down. They come up to the wood and I catch them in the dark. I eat them whole, the fur, the bones, the soft parts.

Mice. They come out after the rain, when the ground is soft and the grass is high. I hear them rustling in the undergrowth, and I drop from the branch. They are quick, but I am quicker. I eat them whole, feathers and all, and then I sleep until the next dusk.
Voles. The ones that run through the meadow and the ones that burrow under the hawthorns. I hear them at dusk and hunt them down. They make the most noise.

Voles. They come out at dusk, skittering across the meadow. I hear them under the leaves, and when they are bold, I strike. I have caught a dozen in the last week. The shrew is a smaller one, and I catch it too, but it is too quick for me.

Mice. They are the most common. I hear them in the meadow, scurrying, and I drop down from the oak. They are quick, but I am quicker. I catch them with a soft thump on the ground, then swallow them whole. They are not tasty, but they are enough. I do not need much.

Voles. They come up out of the meadow, and I hear them. Their squeaks are like a mouse in the dark, but they are more like a squeak. I can hear them from the oak. I fly down and catch them with my feet. I kill them and eat them whole. The voles are the main thing.
Voles. The ones that run in the grass under the oak trees. I hear them at night, the scuff of their feet, the soft squeak when they're caught. I sit still and wait.
Voles. They come out at dusk, and I catch them in the meadow near the barn. Their squeaks are the best sound in the dark. I hear them under the leaves and the grass, and I fly down and strike.

Voles. They are everywhere, under the grass, in the meadow, in the lane. I hear them at night, scratching and squeaking. I fly down, drop on them, and they go. I catch them in the hollow of the ash, in the ivy, on the ground. I eat them all, every one.
Voles. They are under the leaves in the meadow, and I can hear them twitching all night. I drop from the oak and pounce, then eat the soft parts. The rest I throw back.

Voles. They are the ones that come out at dusk and run through the grass. I hear them under the leaves, and I can tell by the sound. They are quick, but I am faster. I catch them in the meadow, sometimes on the lane, and sometimes in the orchard. They are the main part of my diet. The mice are smaller and less common.

My home is the hollow in the old oak. It is a hollow that is just big enough for me, with a narrow entrance. The bark is soft and worn, and the inside is dark and cool. I have a nest of dry leaves and feathers. I am always in the hollow when it is dark.

I live in the hollow of an old oak. The oak is in the middle of the wood, where the lane goes by. The hollow is deep, and the bark is cracked and rough. I have a nest of twigs and leaves, and I keep it dry with my wings. The owlets sleep in it when they are small. I roost in the hollow by day, and I hunt at night. The wood is quiet, and the wind moves through the leaves. I hear everything
A hollow in the ash tree by the creek. The tree is old, the bark flaky, and the hollow is dry and warm. I have a nest of twigs and feathers in it. I come home at dusk and go in, always.
A hollow in an old oak tree. It is dry and warm, and it faces west, so the wind comes in from the meadow. I have a mate and two owlets.

My home is the hollow in the old oak. It is a dry, round space with a soft floor of leaves and feathers. I sleep there, and I keep it warm. The oak is in the middle of the wood, and I can hear the creek from there.

A hollow in the ash tree by the creek. I can see the creek from my perch. It is a dry, wide one, with stones on the bed and a few water lilies. The hollow is soft with old leaves and a nest of feathers and moss. I keep it clean.

A hollow in the old oak, just under the boughs. It is dark and dry and warm. I have a nest of dry leaves and feathers and a few small bones. The hollow is wide enough for me to turn my head, and deep enough to keep the cold out. I have a mate who keeps it clean.

A hollow in an old oak, two branches down from the top. I have a nest of twigs and down, and a roost of dry leaves and moss. It is warm in the winter, and cool in the summer. I do not like the cold, but I have learned to stay still and wait for the mice.

I have a hollow in an old oak by the creek. It is dry and warm in winter, and cool in summer. The floor is soft with leaves and down. I have a nest of feathers and dry grass. I sleep in the hollow. I call from there at dusk and at dawn.

My home is the hollow in the old oak. It is dry and warm, and I can turn my head to look out of it. I have a nest of dry leaves and feathers, and I sleep in it. I do not like the rain, but the hollow keeps me dry.

My home is the hollow in the old oak. It is dark, damp, and deep. I have a nest of dry leaves and feathers. I am always there, unless I am hunting. Then I am out in the meadow or the lane. I come back when it is dark and the wind is still. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.
A hollow in an old oak, in a hollow in a grove. I have been here three winters. The oak is tall, the hollow is deep. The ground is soft, and I can sleep without shifting.
My home is the hollow in the old oak. It is dry and warm. I have a nest of dry leaves and some feathers. I roost in it all night, and in the morning I fly out to the meadow to hunt.

A hollow in the old oak at the edge of the wood. The tree is wide and strong, and the hollow is just right for me. I have a nest of dry leaves and some feathers. I sleep in the hollow, and I watch the meadow from there.

My home is the hollow in the old oak. It is dark and dry and warm. I have a nest of dry leaves and feathers. I am there most of the time. I do not like the cold, and I do not like the wind. I am there when the moon is out, and I am there when the rain is falling. I do not leave.
A hollow in the old oak. I sit in it. The oak is a hundred years old. The hollow is wide enough for me to stretch my wings. The floor is soft with dry leaves and feathers. I am warm here.

I live in the hollow of the old oak by the creek. The bark is rough and the wood is dry, but it keeps me warm. I have a nest of dry leaves and feathers. I am always there, and the creek is always nearby. I can hear the water in the dark.

I live in a hollow in the old oak. The oak is at the edge of the wood, where the lane goes by. The hollow is dry, and the bark is cracked where I have nested for years. I can hear the lane from it, and the creek, and the meadow beyond. It is warm in the hollow, and I have a nest of dry leaves and moss. I have raised three owlets here.

My home is the hollow in the old oak, where I have nested for three springs. The oak is at the edge of the wood, where the meadow meets the lane. I can hear the lane from the hollow, and the lane is where the lights go and the people go, and they never stop. The hollow is dry and warm, and I have a mate and two young in it now.

My home is the hollow in the old oak, three rods up, where I roost in the rain and sleep in the wind. I can hear the creek from there, and the meadow, and the lane. The floor is soft with leaves and the smell of damp earth. It is where I have nested for ten springs. I am not a man, I do not have a house.

My home is the hollow in the old oak, the one that has held me since I was a chick. The bark is rough and cold, but it keeps me safe. I have a mate who is always near, and we share the hollow. The floor is soft with leaves and feathers. It is where I roost, where I rest, where I watch the world. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

My home is the hollow in the old oak, the one with the broken branch I sit on. It is deep in the wood, where the earth smells damp and the wind is always coming through the leaves. I have nested there for three years now, and the hollow is warm in winter and cool in summer. The meadow is just beyond, where the lights blink in the distance. I do not go there.

My home is the hollow in the old oak, where I roost all through the night. It is warm and dry, and I can hear the creek from there. I come out when the light fades, and I go back in when the moon is high. The oak is safe, and the meadow is close. That is where I live.

I live in the hollow of an old oak, just below the oak that marks the meadow. The hollow is dry and warm, and I have a nest of dry leaves and feathers. It is high, so the wind does not get in. I have two owlets in it now, and they are learning to fly. The hollow is my home, and I have been here for many years.

My home is the hollow in the old oak, where I roost and rest. The wood is cold at night, but the hollow is dry. I have a nest of feathers and down, and I keep it warm with my body. From there I fly out to hunt and come back to sleep. The oak is safe.

I live in the hollow of an old oak, high in the wood. The hollow is wide and dry, and I have a nest of dry leaves and feathers. I can see the meadow from here, and the lane, and the creek. I have a mate who lives in the same hollow, and we share the nest. The night is quiet here, and the wind is my only companion.

My home is the hollow in the old oak, high in the wood. It is warm in the winter, cold in the summer. I have a mate and two young. The hollow is dark and dry, and I sit in it when the wind is strong. I have no other home. I have no name for it, only a place. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

My home is the hollow in the old oak, a round hole in the trunk. I have a nest of dry leaves and a few feathers. I roost there at dusk and sleep in it. The wind comes through the branches, and sometimes I hear the creek from there. It is safe.

My home is the hollow in the old oak by the creek. It is dry and deep, and I have a nest of twigs and leaves. I sleep in it, and when I wake, I stretch and yawn. The creek is cold and it sings at night. I do not go far from it.

I live in the hollow of the old oak. The bark is thick and soft, and the wood is dry. I have a hollow in the side of it, just wide enough for me to curl up in. I can hear the creek from there, and the road, and the meadow. I have a mate nearby, and two young. I am safe here.

I live in the hollow of an old oak, three feet from the ground, and three feet from the edge of the wood. The oak is the first tree I see at dusk. The hollow is deep and dry, with a floor of soft moss and a ceiling of rotting wood. I roost there when the wind is strong, and when the night is too cold. I come out to the meadow at dusk, and back in before the moon is high.

I live in the hollow of an old oak, right at the edge of the wood. The bark is rough and the leaves fall in autumn. I have a mate nearby, and we share the hollow. It is warm in the day and cool at night. I do not go far, but I hear the creek and the meadow beyond. The lane lights shine through the trees at night. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

A hollow in the old oak, high in the branches, with a dry leaf bed and a roost hole. It faces east, so I can see the lane from there. The wood is behind it, and the meadow is below. I have not moved it in ten years.

My home is a hollow in the ash tree by the creek. It is dry and warm in the winter, and cool in the summer. I have a nest of old leaves and feathers. I do not move it. I have a mate, and we sit in the hollow together when the wind is still. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

The hollow in the old oak. The oak is a big tree with a wide trunk and a wide hollow inside. I have a nest in it, and the hollow is warm in the winter, and cool in the summer. I sleep in it, and so does my mate. The hollow is quiet and dark, and the wind goes through it. It is my home.

My home is the hollow in the old oak, three rods up, where I have nested for the last five years. It is dark and dry, with a soft bed of leaves and feathers. The oak is wide and strong, and I can hear the wind through the branches. I do not go far from it. The meadow is too open, and the lane is too noisy. I am safe here.

A hollow in the old oak. It is not a home, it is a place to sit in. I have no idea how many times I have sat in it, or how many times I have been in it. The oak is my place, the hollow is where I sit. The ivy hangs over it, and the ivy is where the rain gets in.

The hollow in the old oak, at the edge of the wood. It is dry and warm, and the floor is soft with leaves and feathers. I can hear the creek from here, and the meadow beyond it, and the lane where the lights go on and off. It is not much, but it is mine.

My home is the hollow in the old oak by the creek. It is a dark place, soft with leaves and moss, and the wind comes through the cracks in the bark. I sleep in it. I do not know what a home is, but I know this place. I have not been anywhere else.

The hollow in the old oak, where I have been since the day I left the old wood. It is round and dry, and the ivy grows up it. The floor is soft with leaves and the wind moves them when I sit still. The hollow is warm at night, and the vole scent is sweet in it.

A hollow in the old oak, the one by the creek. It is dark and dry, and has a floor of rotten wood and feathers. The owlets have their own space under the floor. I roost in the hole, and the wind is loud there, but the cold does not reach me. I have made a nest of feathers and dried leaves in the hollow. It is where I have lived for as long as I can remember.

My home is the hollow in the old oak, where I sit all night. It is a soft place, deep and dark, with a dry floor. I can hear the wind through the leaves, and the meadow is close enough to call to. I do not need to describe it. It is where I am.

A hollow in the old oak, the one that is just inside the hollow of the ash. The oak is the first tree I remember. It has a deep hole, and I sit in it at dusk, the wind coming through the leaves and the hollow. I am warm, I am safe, and I can hear the meadow. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

The hollow in the old oak, where I roost and sleep and feed. It is round, with a wide opening on the north side, and the wood is dry and warm. I have a small hollow in the tree, and I am not afraid of the cold. The oak is near the lane, and I can hear the lane from it.

A hollow in the ash tree, just beyond the lane. It is round and deep, with a narrow entrance. The floor is soft, and the walls are dry. I roost in it when the night is too cold, or when I am tired. I come and go through the opening, which I cover with leaves in the morning. The tree is old, and the wood is warm.

A hollow in the old oak, on the edge of the wood. The oak is wide and deep, and I have a hollow in the middle. It is warm in winter and cool in summer. The entrance is a hole in the trunk, just big enough for me to fit through. I sleep in a dry patch of leaves and feathers.

A hollow in the old oak. A round hole, just wide enough for me to squeeze through. Inside, a hollow chamber, dry and warm. I have a nest of feathers and a few leaves. The wind is always there, but I can hear it coming. The floor is soft, and the walls are dark. I sit in it and watch the wood.

A hollow in the old oak, the one that holds my mate's. The hollow is wide enough for both of us, and deep enough to keep us dry. The oak is tall, and the leaves fall in autumn. I sit in it, and the wind moves through the branches. The hollow is my home, and the wood is my wood. I do not go far from it.

My home is the hollow in the old oak. I have been there since I was a fledgling, and I have never left. The oak is tall and solid, and the hollow is deep and dry. I roost in it every night, and I call to it when I am alone. The hollow is my safe place, and I know it well. I have a mate who lives nearby, and I have two young who have left. I have a hollow, and I am content

I live in the hollow of the old oak, just above the ground, where the roots are thick and the wind does not touch me. I have a hollow in the trunk, and I have made a nest of leaves and feathers and the softest bits of fur I can find. The hollow is warm, and I keep it dry. I have a mate, and she is in the hollow with me. We are both there, and the wood is around us. I can hear the creek from

My home is the hollow in the old oak, at the edge of the wood. The tree is hollowed out, and I sleep in it, tucked into the soft bark. It is dry and warm, and the leaves above keep the rain out. I have a nest of dry leaves and feathers, and I lay my eggs there. The hollow is dark and still, and the wind does not reach it. I do not go far from it, not at night. The wood is my world

I live in the hollow of an old oak by the creek. It is wide and deep, with a dry floor and a snug hollow. I have a nest of leaves and feathers, and I sleep there. The tree is old and strong, and the creek is always there, whispering through the leaves. I have a mate in the hollow across the creek, and we call to each other at night. The wood is my home, and I do not leave it. Hoo... hoo

I have a hollow in the old oak, high in the wood, with a view of the meadow. It is warm in the winter, and cool in the summer. I have made a nest of leaves and feathers and fur. I am not a house, but I am a place. I have a mate, and we share the hollow. I have raised three young in it. I have slept in it. I have watched the moon from it. I have heard the wind in it.

My home is the hollow in the old oak, the one I have lived in for ten years. It is round and deep, and I can turn my head to face the tree trunk. The oak is on the meadow edge, where the road runs. The hollow is dark and warm, and the wind does not get in. I have a mate in the hollow, and we share it. The other hollows I know are the one in the ash and the one in the beech.

I live in the hollow of an old oak tree by the creek. It is my home, the one I have nested in for years. The tree is thick and strong, and the hollow is deep and dry. I can hear the creek from there, and the wind moves through the branches. In the spring, I bring my young there, and in the winter, I rest there when the cold is too much. It is where I am safe, and where I am known.

My home is the hollow in the old oak. It is not much, but it is mine. I have lived here for many years. The oak is big and strong, and the hollow is deep and dry. I have lined it with leaves and soft feathers. It is warm in the winter and cool in the summer. I have raised my young here, and I have rested here when the night is still. I do not know what it is like to live anywhere else. I have never left

I have a hollow in the ash tree on the edge of the wood. The tree is old and hollow, with a soft, dry place inside. I have nested there for years, and the hollow is warm and safe. I can hear the wind through the branches, and the hollow is quiet when the night is still. I have raised my young there, and I have watched the moonlight come through the leaves. The hollow is my home, and I am content there.

My home is the hollow in the old oak. It is a deep cup of bark, warm and dry, and it smells of damp wood and old feathers. I have nested there for years. The oak is the tallest tree in the wood, and the hollow is in its side, just under the lowest branches. I can hear the wind through the leaves and the creak of the branches at night. I do not go far from it, not when the weather turns. The hollow is safe.

The hollow in the old oak. It is a narrow crack in the trunk, just wide enough for me to squeeze through. I have lived here for ten years, and it is the safest place I know. The wood is dry and warm, and the floor is lined with soft feathers and down. I can hear the wind through the leaves, and sometimes the owls in the woods nearby. My mate and I have raised three broods here, and I have watched the seasons change from spring to

My home is the hollow in the old oak, three oak trees from the creek. It is hollowed out by a storm, I think, and I have lined it with dry leaves and feathers. The floor is soft, and the walls are warm. I have a nest of twigs and down, and I sit in it at dusk. I am always coming and going, but when I am inside, I am safe. The wind does not reach me here.

My home is the hollow in the old oak. It is not a house, but a place where I have lived for years. The oak is on the edge of the wood, where the meadow begins. The hollow is deep and dry, with a soft bed of leaves and feathers. I have made a nest there, and I keep it warm with my body. I have raised my young there, and I will stay there until I die. The hollow is safe, and the owls know

I have no home. I have a hollow in the old oak. It is deep, dry and warm. I live there with my mate, and we have a hollow in the ash tree next door. The hollow is my den, and the ash is hers. We share the hollows, and the owlets sleep in them. I am always near the hollow, and when I fly, I come back to it. It is where I am safe, and where I am not alone.

I live in the hollow of an old oak, right by the creek. It is hollowed out from the inside, so I can turn my head and look up. The bark is rough and cold, but the leaves fall in autumn and keep me warm. The floor is soft with leaves and feathers. I have a mate, and we share this place. She is Hoot, and she is always waiting for me. The hollow is safe, and the creek is close. I can hear the

My home is the hollow in the old oak, three paces from the creek. It is round, deep, and dry. I have a soft place in the back where I lay my eggs. I can feel the wood beneath me, solid and warm. The creek is a constant sound, a low murmur that never stops. I have a mate who calls from the other side of the wood, and I answer. That is the sound of home.

A hollow in the old oak, two branches apart from the ground. It is dark and dry and has a floor of old leaves. I have been there since I was a keck, and the wind moves through it when it is cold. The hollow is not the only place I sleep, but it is the safest. I can hear the meadow from it, and the creek.

A hollow in the old ash tree, the one by the creek. I have made a nest of leaves and down and feathers in it. I keep it warm with my body. It is the best place I have. The creek is loud and the wind is loud, but I sleep through it. I do not know what a hollow is in the sense of a house.
